newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Kabila encounters some dissent in Shaba.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Kabila encounters some dissent in Shaba.

text.p: Rebel leader Laurent Kabila remained in seclusion in Lubumbashi on Tuesday, 24 hours after he arrived to mark the capture of Zaire's second city.

Lubumbashi's one million people were still awaiting a rally, a victory parade or even a clear glimpse of Kabila, who swept into town on Monday in Mercedes jeep with dark-tinted windows, in the middle of a convoy of soldiers.

The only political show in town was a demonstration by several hundred people who welcomed Kabila but at the same time denounced him for imposing an interim governor on Shaba province instead of holding quick elections here as elsewhere.
The man they supported, incumbent governor Kyungu wa Kumwanza, did not appear at the demonstration and there were unconfirmed rumours that he was under house arrest.

Kabila, Kyungu and the interim governor, Gaetan Kakudji, grew up together in the same village in Shaba, known to its people by the old name, Katanga province. But they have clearly travelled different political routes.
The delay and the dissent in Lubumbashi were unusual.
Kabila has usually appeared quickly in public during victory visits to towns in the centre and east as they were captured by rebel forces.
A news conference called for Monday evening failed to take place and Kabila officials offered no explanation.
One source said the leader of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) was too busy seeing businessmen to meet the press.

About a dozen white businessmen were lodged at the city's main hotel, including some big players in the diamond and minerals industry. The AFDL says it intends to break up monopoly deals in the industry and renegotiate contracts.

Demonstrators outside the hotel, a temporary base of some senior Kabila officials, said they would continue their protest and possibly call for a strike if Kabila refused to call elections or give them an explanation.

"We're disappointed with this," said spokesman Gustave Kakala N'goy. "We don't like these methods. We should have an election and if Kyungu should lose then fine. But we want democracy not dictatorship."
The nationalist Katangese party says governor Kyungu helped Kabila's rebels to take Lubumbashi with few casualties by persuading the Zaire army to change sides.
Critics of the Shaba governor say he is simply an opportunist attempting to jump on the Kabila bandwagon, evidently without success so far.
